title-group.article-title: Cramér-Rao Bounds for Wideband Near-Field Sensing

institution-wrap.institution: Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust (SnT)

abstract.p: The evolution of array signal processing technologies is progressing toward the deployment of compact, densely arranged sensors to form extremely large aperture arrays (ELAA), aiming to significantly improve angular resolution and beamforming gain. In this paper, we propose a wideband near-field sensing system that combines orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signaling with ELAA technology. The ELAA transmitter emits wideband signals, while the radar receiver processes the echoes to estimate critical target parameters, including location, velocity, and radar cross-section. We then derive the generalized Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRB) to assess the OFDM system’s estimation performance. Numerical experiments reveal that the proposed wideband near-field sensing system outperforms its far-field and narrowband counterparts by achieving lower CRB values.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Extremely large-scale antenna arrays (ELAA) and extremely high frequencies (EHF) are set to play a transformative role in enabling sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems [1], [2]. These systems aim to provide ultra-reliable, low-latency communication, massive connectivity, ultra-high data rates, and precise positioning [3]. These advancements also pave the way for integrating sensing capabilities into 6G networks, addressing critical challenges such as spectrum congestion, hardware costs, and power consumption [4]–[8]. However, the combination of ELAA and EHF extends the Rayleigh distance, necessitating operation in the near-field region [9]. This shift underscores the need for accurate near-field signal models and sophisticated processing algorithms to fully harness the potential of these technologies [10].

With the advent of ELAA-EHF systems, it is essential to benchmark their performance. Lower bounds on estimation errors are critical for evaluating the performance of both radar [11] and communication [12] systems. A widely adopted metric is the Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRB), which defines the theoretical limit on the variance of an estimator for unknown parameters [13]. The CRB is particularly tight when estimation errors are small [14]. In communication systems, CRB is commonly applied for evaluating channel state information (CSI) estimation. For instance, [12] derives the CRB for a far-field MIMO-OFDM communication system, while [15] explores the CRB for near-field communication scenarios. However, communication-based channel estimation often targets composite quantities rather than specific parameters like the position, velocity, or reflectivity of users (LoS paths) and background scatterers (NLoS paths). These tasks, typically addressed by radar systems, have been explored through various CRBs, including those for direction of arrival (DOA) estimation [16].

For systems leveraging wideband processing, CRBs have been developed for far-field wideband DOA estimation [17] and range-Doppler estimation [18]. While far-field systems can decouple parameters like DOA and range for separate processing, near-field systems face challenges in decoupling these parameters due to their inherent coupling. In [19], the CRB for narrowband MIMO radar systems is proposed for static targets, evaluating estimation performance along individual axes. However, existing methods often overlook the combined gains of wideband and near-field processing, particularly for non-static targets.

To address these limitations, we propose a wideband near-field sensing system utilizing OFDM transmission for non-static objects. The CRB is analyzed for key parameters, including location, velocity, and radar cross-section (RCS), within this wideband framework. Unlike prior works such as [20], which focus on static targets in narrowband setups, our approach evaluates the CRB for both velocity and RCS estimation of moving targets in a wideband configuration. Furthermore, the proposed wideband near-field CRB is benchmarked against far-field narrowband [21], far-field wideband [17], and near-field narrowband [19] schemes. Our findings highlight that target velocity significantly impacts position estimation. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed wideband near-field sensing system achieves a lower CRB compared to its counterparts, showcasing its superiority for next-generation sensing applications.

sec.title: SYSTEM MODEL
sec.p: Consider a wideband MIMO radar sensing system employing the OFDM signaling and ELAA, comprising a transmitter (Tx) with Nt-antenna uniform linear array (ULA) and a receiver (Rx) with Nr-antenna ULA; the Tx and Rx can be co-located or separately deployed. Let ${{\mathbb{I}}_{{n_t}}} = \left({{x_{{n_t}}},{y_{{n_t}}}}\right),{n_t} \in \left\{ {1, \cdots ,{N_t}} \right\}{\text{and}}\,{{\mathbb{I}}_{{n_r}}} = \left({{x_{{n_r}}},{y_{{n_r}}}}\right),{n_r} \in \left\{ {1, \cdots ,{N_r}} \right\}$ denote the position of nt-th Tx antenna and nr-th Rx antenna, respectively, in a two-dimensional (2-D) Cartesian plane. The near-field coverage area comprises Q targets, a term which refers to the objects of interest to radar, communication users, and scatterers; the q-th target located at Iq and having a velocity v(q), q = 1, ⋯, Q.

The OFDM signaling involves K subcarriers, M OFDM symbols each of which has a total duration of Tsym = Tcp + Tes, where Tcp and Tes denote the cyclic prefix duration and the elementary symbol duration, respectively, and $\Delta f = \frac{1}{{{T_{{\text{es}}}}}}$ denotes the subcarrier spacing. Further, Tcpi = MTsym denotes the frame length of the coherent processing interval (CPI) [22].

We consider frequency-dependent path loss in (2) which can be modeled as $g_{*,k}^q = \sqrt {{z_*}} \frac{{{\lambda _k}}}{{4\pi \left\| {{{\mathbb{I}}_q} - {{\mathbb{I}}_*}} \right\|}}$ [27], [28], where ∗ ∈ {nr, nt}, z∗ denotes radiation profile of the material of corresponding element, and z∗ = 1 for the full-digital array and 0 < z∗ < 1 for metasurface array [19]. We consider the z∗ = 1 case in this paper for simplicity.

Following [23], [24], we then assume that the Doppler-related phase-shift within an OFDM symbol duration is negligible, i.e., $f_{{n_t}{n_r}}^{q,k} \ll \frac{1}{{{T_{{\text{sym}}}}}} < \frac{1}{{{T_{{\text{es}}}}}} = \vartriangle f,{\text{hence}}\,f_{{n_t}{n_r}}^{q,k}t \approx f_{{n_t}{n_r}}^{q,k}m{T_{{\text{sym}}}},t \in \left[ {m{T_{{\text{sym}}}},(m + 1){T_{{\text{sym}}}}} \right]$. Further, this causes no inter-carrier interference. Removing CP and the carrier frequency in I/Q demodulation and implementing the Fourier transform within m-th time interval i.e., OFDM symbol duration, the received signal on the k-th subcarrier of the m-th OFDM symbol is given by \begin{equation*}{y_{{n_r}}}[m,k] = \int_{m{T_{{\text{sym}}}} + {T_{{\text{cp}}}}}^{(m + 1){T_{{\text{sym}}}}} {{y_{{n_r}}}} (t){e^{ - 2\pi {f_c}t}}{e^{ - 2\pi k\Delta ft}}dt.\tag{5}\end{equation*}

Substituting (2) into (5) and stacking the received signal of all the Rx elements, we have (5) as \begin{align*}& {{\mathbf{y}}_{k,m}} = \sum\limits_{q = 1}^Q {{\alpha _q}} {{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{R}}}(k,m,q){\mathbf{a}}_{\text{T}}^T(k,m,q){{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}} + {{\mathbf{n}}_{k,m}},{\text{where}} \\ & {{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{T}}}(k,m,q) = {\left[ {g_{1,k}^q{e^{j2\pi {\varphi _1}(k,m,q)}}, \cdots ,g_{{N_t},k}^q{e^{j2\pi {\varphi _{{N_t}}}(k,m,q)}}} \right]^T}, \\ & {\varphi _*}(k,m,q) = \frac{{{f_k}}}{c}\left({\frac{{\left\langle {{{\mathbf{v}}^{(q)}},{{\mathbb{I}}_q} - {{\mathbb{I}}_*}} \right\rangle }}{{\left\| {{{\mathbb{I}}_q} - {{\mathbb{I}}_*}} \right\|}}m{T_{{\text{sym}}}} - \left\| {{{\mathbb{I}}_q} - {{\mathbb{I}}_*}} \right\|}\right),* \in \left\{ {{n_t},{n_r}} \right\}.\tag{6}\end{align*}

sec.title: WIDEABND NEAR-FIELD CRB ANALYSIS
sec.p: Let us first rewrite (8) as the real vector ${\overline {\mathbf{y}} _k} = {\left[ {\Re {{\left({{{\mathbf{y}}_k}}\right)}^T};\Im {{\left({{{\mathbf{y}}_k}}\right)}^T}} \right]^T},{\overline {\mathbf{\mu }} _k} = {\left[ {\Re {{\left({{{\mathbf{\mu }}_k}}\right)}^T},\Im {{\left({{{\mathbf{\mu }}_k}}\right)}^T}} \right]^T},{\text{and}}\,{\overline {\mathbf{C}} _k} = \frac{{\sigma _r^2}}{2}{{\mathbf{I}}_{2{N_r}M}}$ To evaluate CRB, we can first write the likelihood function of as [29] \begin{equation*}{p_k}\left({{{\overline {\mathbf{y}} }_k},{\mathbf{\theta }}}\right) = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {2{\pi ^{2{N_r}M}}\left| {{{\overline {\mathbf{C}} }_k}} \right|} }}{e^{ - {{\left({{{\overline {\mathbf{y}} }_k} - {{\bar \mu }_k}}\right)}^T}\overline {\mathbf{C}} _k^{ - 1}\left({{{\overline {\mathbf{y}} }_k} - {{\bar \mu }_k}}\right)/2}}.\tag{10}\end{equation*}

According to (10), we can write the log-likelihood function and omit the constant terms as \begin{equation*}\ln {p_k}\left({{{\overline {\mathbf{y}} }_k},{\mathbf{\theta }}}\right) = - \frac{1}{2}\left({\ln \left| {{{\overline {\mathbf{C}} }_k}} \right| + {{\left({{{\overline {\mathbf{y}} }_k} - {{\overline {\mathbf{\mu }} }_k}}\right)}^T}\overline {\mathbf{C}} _k^{ - 1}\left({{{\overline {\mathbf{y}} }_k} - {{\overline {\mathbf{\mu }} }_k}}\right)}\right).\tag{11}\end{equation*}

CRB for RCS Estimation: Based on (7), we have, for q = 1, ⋯,Q, \begin{align*}&\frac{{\partial {{\mathbf{A}}_{k,m}}{{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}}}}{{\partial {\alpha _{{R_q}}}}} = {{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{R}}}(k,m,q){\mathbf{a}}_{\text{T}}^T(k,m,q){{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}},\tag{16a} \\ & \frac{{\partial {{\mathbf{A}}_{k,m}}{{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}}}}{{\partial {\alpha _{{I_q}}}}} = j{{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{R}}}(k,m,q){\mathbf{a}}_{\text{T}}^T(k,m,q){{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}}.\tag{16b}\end{align*}

Substituting (19) into (14) and (13), the CRB related to the velocity estimation of q-th target is \begin{align*}& {\operatorname{CRB} _{{v_{{x_q}}},L}} = \frac{{\sigma _r^2}}{{2\sum _{k = 1}^K\sum _{m = 1}^M\left\| {{{\mathbf{{\acute{A}}}}_{k,m}}(q){{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}}} \right\|_2^2}},\tag{21a} \\ {\operatorname{CRB} _{{v_{{y_q}}},L}} = \frac{{\sigma _r^2}}{{2\sum _{k = 1}^K\sum _{m = 1}^M\left\| {{{\mathbf{A}}_{k,m}}(q){{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}}} \right\|_2^2}}. \tag{21b}\end{align*}

Single Target Setting: Herein, we consider the single target setup and restrict the transmit power in each OFDM symbol, i.e., ${\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}^H{{\mathbf{x}}_{k,m}} = {\mathcal{P}}$, where ${\mathcal{P}}$ denotes the transmit power at each subcarrier and OFDM symbol. Note that the MIMO radar in wideband far-field [17], and narrowband near-field [19] cases only consider the static target which limits its application. Towards this end, the performance of CRB of proposed wideband near-field system under moving target setup is investigated. Hereafter, we use the abbreviation NFF, WFF, NNF, and WNF denote narrowband far-field, wideband far-field, narrowband near-field, and wideband near-field, respectively.

Further, we can also have the following inequalities \begin{equation*}{\text{CRB}}_{\alpha ,L}^{{\text{WNF}}} \leq {\text{CRB}}_{\alpha ,L}^{{\text{WFF}}} \leq {\text{CRB}}_{\alpha ,L}^{{\text{NFF}}};{\text{CRB}}_{\alpha ,L}^{{\text{WNF}}} \leq {\text{CRB}}_{\alpha ,L}^{{\text{NNF}}}.\end{equation*}

Similarly, we can approximate the CRB for location estimation in (24) and velocity estimation in (21) using the distance between target and array as in (25) and (27), respectively. This is omitted for lack of space. Meanwhile, estimating the parameters, i.e, RCS, velocity and location of all targets is beyond the scope of this paper and will be investigated in the full version of this paper.

sec.title: NUMERICAL EXPERIMENTS
sec.p: In the simulations, we consider a bistatic MIMO radar system with Nt = Nr = 128. The inter-element spacing for both Tx and Rx is set to λc/2. The central frequency of the wideband sensing system is fc = 28 GHz, and the frequency step of OFDM is set to Δf = 0.12 MHz. The total number of subcarriers and OFDM symbols are set to K = 8 and M = 64. A single target is located on the y-axis and moves with a velocity of v = [10], [10] m/s. The RCS is set to α = 1. The noise variances are $\sigma _r^2$ = 154dBm.

Fig. 1 illustrates the CRB of RCS estimation versus the transmit power of each element. We compare the proposed wideband near-field sensing system with its far-field narrowband [21], far-field wideband [17], and near-field narrowband [19] counterparts. It is observed that as transmit power increases, the CRB for RCS decreases linearly, consistent with our analysis in (25) and (27). Meanwhile, a target located in the near-field region achieves a lower RCS estimation CRB compared to the far-field region. This is because, in the near-field region, free-space path loss is always smaller than in the far-field region. Further, in the extremely near-field region, e.g., 2.5m, the approximation in (27) is more accurate than the approximation in (25). Finally, the wideband CRBs are always lower than the narrowband CRBs due to the wideband processing gain, despite requiring more spectrum resources.

Fig. 2 illustrates the CRB of velocity estimation versus the transmit power of each element. Similarly, it is observed that as transmit power increases, the CRB for velocity also decreases linearly across different cases. Meanwhile, when the target is located in the near-field region, it achieves a lower velocity estimation CRB compared to a target in the far-field region since we can only obtain radial velocity in far-field. Furthermore, as the target distance decreases, a lower CRB is always achieved due to the higher Tx and Rx channel gain in (21). Moreover, the CRB for the far-field is still not favorable, even with high transmit power, i.e., ${\mathcal{P}}$ = 40 dBm. This means that to reach the same estimation accuracy, we need to improve transmit power or use more subcarriers, i.e., increase the bandwidth. Finally, the wideband CRBs for velocity are always lower than the corresponding narrowband counterparts due to the wideband processing gain, i.e., K > 1 for the summation of channel gain in wideband systems, but K = 1 for the narrowband case.

caption.p: Transmit power versus CRB for velocity estimation.
Transmit power versus CRB for location estimation.

sec.p: Fig. 3 illustrates the CRB of location estimation versus the transmit power of each element. Similar to Fig. 2, we observe that as transmit power increases, the CRB for location also decreases linearly in all cases. Finally, as the target distance decreases, i.e., from the far-field to the near-field and then to the extremely near-field region, the CRB is always reduced due to the higher Tx and Rx channel gain in (24).

sec.title: SUMMARY
sec.p: In this paper, we studied a wideband near-field sensing system using ELAA and OFDM signaling. We analyze the CRB for estimating RCS, velocity, and location of the radar target. Based on the analysis, the considered wideband near-field sensing system achieves a lower CRB compared to its far-field narrowband [21], far-field wideband [17], and near-field narrowband [19] counterparts. Meanwhile, the performance of CRBs largely depends on the target distance. Numerical simulation results validate our analysis and show that the proposed system achieves a lower CRB than other schemes.
